title: Finlandia
hook: Music written for a protest against Russian censorship, with a quiet hymn at its heart that became Finland’s second anthem.

painting.title: Washing on the Ice
painting.collection: Ateneum Art Museum, Finnish National Gallery, Helsinki
painting.pairingNote: A woman rinses laundry through a hole in the lake ice, painted in 1900, the year Finlandia was first performed; Halonen belonged to the same circle of Finnish artists as Sibelius, who were turning their country’s life and landscape into art.

facts: In 1899 Finland was a grand duchy of the Russian Empire, and that February the emperor issued a manifesto that cut back its self-government. Censorship of the press grew. In November the Finnish newspapers organised the Press Celebrations in Helsinki, a covert patriotic protest.
The evening included a series of tableaux from Finnish history, from the time of the Kalevala onwards. Sibelius wrote the music. The last tableau was called “Finland Awakes”.

He reworked that final number into a separate piece, first performed in Helsinki on 2 July 1900 by the Helsinki Philharmonic Society under Robert Kajanus. The name *Finlandia*, suggested by Sibelius’s friend Axel Carpelan, came into use soon after. Under Russian rule the piece is said to have been played at times under harmless titles such as “Impromptu”.

The quiet hymn in the middle is often taken for a folk tune, but it is Sibelius’s own. In 1941 the poet Veikko Antero Koskenniemi set words to it, and as the “Finlandia Hymn” it is sung in Finland almost as a second national anthem. With other words it is also a church hymn in many countries, for example “Be Still, My Soul”.
bigPicture.inOneLine: dark, menacing brass (the oppression), a call to struggle, a confident fast march, a hymn of hope, and a blazing end.

movements.heading: Finlandia
movements.summary: A [[symphonic-poem|symphonic poem]] in one movement, built like a story: from darkness, through struggle, to light. It opens with heavy, groaning chords in the brass, answered by plaintive woodwinds. A hammering rhythm calls to battle, a confident fast section follows, and then everything stops for a quiet hymn. The fast music returns and drives to a triumphant ending.

mainIdeas.name: The brass chords
mainIdeas.description: low, heavy and dark, in an unclear key, like a weight pressing down.

mainIdeas.name: The call
mainIdeas.description: a short, stamping rhythm in the brass over rolling timpani.

mainIdeas.name: The hymn
mainIdeas.description: a calm, noble melody in long notes, first in the woodwinds, then in the strings.

stops.hear: Slow, heavy chords in the brass, dark and threatening
stops.happening: The opening: the weight of oppression

stops.hear: The woodwinds answer softly, like a lament
The strings take over, dark and searching, with the timpani rumbling below
Faster: the brass hammer out a short, stamping rhythm over a drum roll; cymbals crash
stops.happening: Allegro moderato: the call to struggle

stops.hear: The music brightens into a major key; a confident, striding tune, the brass answering the strings
stops.happening: Allegro: the fast main section, in A-flat major

stops.hear: Everything calms. The woodwinds play a slow, noble melody, like a [[chorale|chorale]]
The strings take up the hymn, warmer and fuller

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: The brass blaze out and the piece ends on broad, triumphant chords

notice: Listen for the moment the hymn begins. After so much noise, the orchestra drops to a hush, and the tune sounds like voices singing together.
Compare the brass at the start and at the end. The same instruments that sounded threatening now sound triumphant.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Karajan recorded *Finlandia* with the Berlin Philharmonic for Deutsche Grammophon in 1964, and again, digitally, twenty years later. This is the 1984 remake: broad and slow, about nine and a half minutes, where many performances take about eight.

threads.title: Music as protest
threads.body: *Finlandia* was born at a protest against censorship and was heard as a national rallying cry; under Russian rule it reportedly sometimes had to hide behind other titles.

threads.title: From darkness to light
threads.body: The piece moves from heavy minor-key brass to a major-key hymn and a triumphant close, the same journey in eight or nine minutes that some symphonies take an hour to make.

threads.title: A tune that left its piece
threads.body: The hymn now lives on its own, as a Finnish patriotic song and as a church hymn around the world.
